action: Introduce legume-based cover crops (e.g. vetch, clover, cowpea) in rotation
rationale: Legumes fix atmospheric N2 via rhizobia symbiosis, adding 40-120 kg N/ha/yr; root exudates and residue decomposition feed soil microbial communities, raising labile carbon pools. Flowering legumes also provide forage for pollinators.
references: FAO (2015). Soil Organic Carbon: The Hidden Potential.
IPCC (2019). Climate Change and Land, Ch. 6.

action: Establish agroforestry / alley cropping with native N-fixing trees (e.g. Faidherbia albida, Gliricidia)
rationale: Deep-rooted trees lift nutrients from subsoil, create litter-driven carbon accrual, buffer microclimate (reducing evapotranspiration), and form habitat corridors that raise bird/insect species richness in fragmented landscapes.
references: IPCC (2019). Climate Change and Land, Ch. 5.
FAO (2013). Advancing Agroforestry on the Policy Agenda.

action: Restore 10-30 m riparian buffer strips with native woody species
rationale: Buffers intercept nutrient/sediment runoff, lowering stream N/P loading and pollution index; rooted banks stabilise hydrology, improving water availability for aquatic and terrestrial species.
references: Mayer et al. (2007). J. Environ. Qual. 36:871-882.

action: Apply agricultural lime to raise soil pH into the 6.0-7.0 target band
rationale: Correcting acidity increases cation exchange capacity, unlocks P and Mo, and enables rhizobia and earthworm activity that underpin nutrient cycling and soil structure.
references: Havlin et al. (2016). Soil Fertility and Fertilizers, 8th ed.
FAO (2006). Plant Nutrition for Food Security.

action: Transition to no-till / reduced tillage with residue retention
rationale: Reduces oxidative loss of soil organic carbon, preserves fungal hyphal networks (mycorrhizae) that mediate plant nutrient uptake, and lowers CO2 efflux.
references: IPCC (2019). Climate Change and Land, Ch. 5.

action: Plant native flowering hedgerows along field margins
rationale: Provides continuous pollen/nectar resources and nesting habitat, increasing wild bee and hoverfly abundance, and improves pollination services in adjacent crops.
references: Dicks et al. (2015). IPBES Pollinators Assessment.
Garibaldi et al. (2014). Proc. R. Soc. B 281:20141299.

action: Reforest degraded patches with locally native mixed species (not monoculture)
rationale: Mixed-species native planting maximises habitat structural diversity, restores functional guilds (frugivores, insectivores), and accrues carbon in biomass and soil.
